title: Katherine Mansfield, Bliss recast
author: tbr
note: Omotesando gold, a flowering pear on a terrace, and a young wife's perfect evening that turns on a single glance. After Mansfield, Bliss, 1918.

scenes.title: The Omotesando terrace
scenes.reentry: Haruka felt it in the elevator—bliss, absurd and physical, like champagne already in the blood.

breaths.text: Haruka felt it in the elevator—bliss, absurd and physical, like champagne already in the blood. Thirty, married, a child asleep two floors below with the nanny she trusted too much and not enough. Tokyo’s evening pressed soft gold against the glass of the Omotesando tower. She wanted to run, to fling her bag into the air, to tell the concierge that the world had arranged itself correctly for once.

Instead she keyed the apartment and stood in the entry smelling cedar and the florist’s last delivery: white pears of blossom, forced early, stems wrapped in black tape. Kenji would be late; Kenji was always late in a way that announced importance. She moved through the rooms adjusting what did not need adjusting—the linen napkins folded into quiet architecture, the low bowls of citrus, the playlist she would pretend had chosen itself. In the nursery monitor’s gray hush she watched her daughter’s fist open and close, and felt a tenderness so sharp it bordered on fear.

On the terrace the flowering pear stood in its planter like a held breath. Pale, almost silver under the building’s lights. Beyond it, Omotesando’s traffic made a continuous hush, taxis and black cars sliding as if on oil. A neighbor’s wind chime answered nothing. Haruka touched a petal and thought, without irony, that she and the tree understood each other: both ornamental, both briefly exact, both paid for by someone else’s calendar.

Guests arrived in carefully unstudied clothes. The critic who hated sincerity and collected grievances like stamps. The couple who spoke only of ceramic ghosts and Kyoto kilns. And Aya Nishimura—cool, pale, wearing gray that made other people’s colors look effortful. Haruka’s bliss tightened around Aya the way silk tightens when you sit wrong. She had told Kenji that Aya was “interesting,” a word that hid a warmer one. Kenji had shrugged with his mouth and checked his phone.

Dinner was a performance of ease. Candlelight made everyone’s skin expensive. Haruka laughed at the right intervals and felt, under the laugh, a current running toward Aya as if the table were wired. She caught Aya’s eye across the roast and felt, with a shock that was almost erotic, a shared quiet: as if both of them were listening to the same unplayed note. The critic said something cruel about a young painter; Aya did not defend the painter, only tilted her glass, and Haruka loved her for the tilt.

Later, on the terrace, they stood before the pear without speaking. The blossom held. Somewhere a train announced itself and vanished under the city. A plane’s lights crossed the gap between towers. Haruka thought: this is what happiness is—recognition without demand, a secret that does not yet require betrayal to exist. Aya’s shoulder nearly touched hers. The nearly was the whole evening.

Kenji came out with two glasses and the particular smile he used for people he intended to undress with conversation. He spoke to Aya about a gallery opening in Roppongi, a mutual friend who had become a brand, a joke that required leaning close. Haruka watched the lean. She watched Aya’s hand accept the glass. She watched Kenji’s fingers brush Aya’s wrist as if by accident and remain, for half a second, as if by contract. Aya’s eyes flicked—not to Haruka, not away—only inward, toward a room already booked.
The bliss did not leave; it changed temperature. It became a bright cold that made the pear tree look suddenly like stage dressing.
